cases.statement: For a≤b and interval-integrable f, |∫[a,b] f|≤∫[a,b]|f|.
cases.proof_strategy: Use the triangle inequality for the Bochner integral.
sketch_steps: Use the triangle inequality for the Bochner integral.
The endpoint order fixes positive orientation.
Identify the real norm with absolute value.
The absolute-value integrand is integrable by the original premise.

cases.statement: If f is interval-integrable and |f(x)|≤c throughout the unordered interval between a,b, then |∫[a,b]f|≤c|b-a|.
cases.proof_strategy: Restrict the pointwise bound to the integration interval.
sketch_steps: Restrict the pointwise bound to the integration interval.
The integral norm is bounded by the integral of the constant bound.
Its measure is the absolute interval length.
Retain absolute value for either endpoint orientation.

cases.statement: For a<b, a continuous nonnegative function on [a,b] that is positive at some point of [a,b] has strictly positive integral.
cases.proof_strategy: Use continuity to spread strict positivity from the chosen point.
sketch_steps: Use continuity to spread strict positivity from the chosen point.
The strict endpoint order gives a nontrivial interval.
Nonnegativity prevents cancellation elsewhere.
Apply strict positivity of the integral.

cases.statement: On a nondegenerate closed interval, a continuous nonnegative f has integral zero exactly when it vanishes at every point of that interval.
cases.proof_strategy: If f vanishes, integral congruence gives zero.
sketch_steps: If f vanishes, integral congruence gives zero.
Conversely, a nonzero nonnegative value would be strictly positive.
Continuity and positivity at that point force a positive integral.
This contradicts a zero integral, proving pointwise vanishing.

cases.statement: For continuous f on uIcc(a,b) and nonnegative interval-integrable weight g there, some c in uIcc(a,b) satisfies ∫f*g=f(c)∫g, for either interval orientation.
cases.proof_strategy: Continuity bounds f between its interval extrema.
sketch_steps: Continuity bounds f between its interval extrema.
Nonnegative weights preserve the corresponding integral inequalities.
The intermediate value property supplies the weighted average value.
The result also includes zero total weight and equal endpoints.

cases.statement: Every odd real function has total oriented interval integral zero over [-a,a] for every real a; this value identity alone does not assert integrability.
cases.proof_strategy: Substitute x↦-x in the symmetric interval integral.
sketch_steps: Substitute x↦-x in the symmetric interval integral.
Oddness identifies the transformed integrand with -f.
Integral linearity under negation makes the value its own negative.
Over ℝ this forces the value to be zero.

cases.statement: For continuous even f and every real a, the oriented integral from -a to a is twice the integral from 0 to a.
cases.proof_strategy: Reflect the interval from -a to zero to the interval from zero to a.
sketch_steps: Reflect the interval from -a to zero to the interval from zero to a.
Evenness leaves the integrand unchanged.
Continuity supplies integrability for joining the adjacent intervals.
The two equal half-interval integrals add to twice one half.

cases.statement: For a function with real period c, its total oriented integral over one period is independent of the starting point.
cases.proof_strategy: Translate an interval whose length is the period.
sketch_steps: Translate an interval whose length is the period.
Periodicity identifies corresponding function values.
The integral over a complete period is translation invariant.
This identity keeps its totalized meaning without inferring integrability.

cases.statement: For c≠0 and f interval-integrable between ca+d and cb+d, ∫[a,b]f(cx+d)=(1/c)∫[ca+d,cb+d]f; c may be negative.
cases.proof_strategy: Use the affine change of variables y=cx+d.
sketch_steps: Use the affine change of variables y=cx+d.
The slope c is nonzero, so the coordinate change is invertible.
The new endpoints retain orientation when c is negative.
The reciprocal slope gives the factor 1/c without requiring continuity of f.

cases.statement: Interval integrability of a real function implies interval integrability of its absolute value on the same endpoints.
cases.proof_strategy: Use the integrability premise on the unordered integration interval.
sketch_steps: Use the integrability premise on the unordered integration interval.
Apply the norm-integrability theorem.
For real values the norm is the absolute value.
The endpoint orientation does not change integrability.

cases.statement: An interval-integrable f multiplied by a function g continuous on uIcc(a,b) remains interval-integrable.
cases.proof_strategy: A continuous function on the compact interval is bounded there.
sketch_steps: A continuous function on the compact interval is bounded there.
Multiplying an integrable function by this bounded continuous factor preserves integrability.
Apply the interval version of that product result.
No differentiability or global continuity of g is needed.

cases.statement: Reversing the endpoints negates the total oriented interval integral of any real function.
cases.proof_strategy: Use the oriented interval-integral definition.
sketch_steps: Use the oriented interval-integral definition.
Interchange the two endpoints.
The two measure-restricted integrals exchange places.
Their difference is the negative of the original value.

cases.statement: The integral of the difference of two interval-integrable functions is the difference of their integrals.
cases.proof_strategy: Negating an integrable function preserves integrability.
sketch_steps: Negating an integrable function preserves integrability.
Represent the difference as addition of a negation.
Apply linearity under the two integrability premises.
Rewrite the resulting integral sum as a difference.

cases.statement: For continuous f, differentiation of x↦∫[x,b]f at a gives -f(a).
cases.proof_strategy: Reverse the integral to put the variable endpoint on the right.
sketch_steps: Reverse the integral to put the variable endpoint on the right.
The upper-endpoint fundamental theorem gives derivative f(a).
Negate the integral and its derivative.
The fixed upper endpoint b remains unchanged.

cases.statement: If f is continuous and g,h have derivatives u,v at a, then d/dx ∫[g(x),h(x)]f at a equals f(h(a))*v-f(g(a))*u.
cases.proof_strategy: Write the moving interval integral as two integrals from a fixed origin.
sketch_steps: Write the moving interval integral as two integrals from a fixed origin.
Apply the fundamental theorem to each upper-endpoint integral.
Compose with h and g, retaining both endpoint velocities.
Subtract the lower-endpoint contribution from the upper contribution.

cases.statement: If f,g are continuous on uIcc(a,b), have derivatives h,k on its interior, and h,k are interval-integrable, then ∫[a,b](h*g+f*k)=f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a). No endpoint derivatives are required.
cases.proof_strategy: Continuity on the closed interval controls the endpoint values.
sketch_steps: Continuity on the closed interval controls the endpoint values.
Differentiate the product only on the open interval.
The derivative terms are integrable using the continuous multipliers.
Apply the interval fundamental theorem to the product.

cases.statement: If f has continuous derivative h on uIcc(a,b) and g is continuous only on f(image uIcc(a,b)), then ∫[a,b]g(f(x))*h(x)=∫[f(a),f(b)]g.
cases.proof_strategy: Restrict the derivative witness and its continuity to the source interval.
sketch_steps: Restrict the derivative witness and its continuity to the source interval.
Require outer continuity only on the actual image of that interval.
Apply change of variables with the oriented image endpoints.
No global smoothness or monotonicity of the substitution is assumed.

cases.statement: If f∘g is the identity, g is continuous at a, and f has nonzero derivative u at g(a), then g has derivative 1/u at a.
cases.proof_strategy: The composition identity provides a local left inverse for g.
sketch_steps: The composition identity provides a local left inverse for g.
Continuity of g keeps its values near g(a).
The nonzero derivative of f is invertible as a real linear map.
The inverse-function derivative rule yields the reciprocal derivative.

cases.statement: A function continuous on [a,b] with an explicitly positive derivative throughout (a,b) is strictly increasing on [a,b].
cases.proof_strategy: Take any two ordered points of the closed interval.
sketch_steps: Take any two ordered points of the closed interval.
Continuity gives the mean-value theorem its endpoint hypotheses.
Every interior derivative is strictly positive.
The resulting secant slope is positive, proving strict increase.

cases.statement: If f is nondecreasing on ℝ and has derivative u at a, then u≥0.
cases.proof_strategy: Difference quotients of a nondecreasing function have nonnegative sign.
sketch_steps: Difference quotients of a nondecreasing function have nonnegative sign.
Pass that sign to their limit.
The derivative witness identifies that limit with u.
Conclude nonnegativity, without claiming strict positivity.

cases.statement: A differentiable real function whose derivative is nondecreasing on ℝ is globally convex.
cases.proof_strategy: Compare neighboring secant slopes using the mean-value theorem.
sketch_steps: Compare neighboring secant slopes using the mean-value theorem.
Monotonicity orders the intermediate derivative values.
Thus secant slopes increase from left to right.
The ordered-slope criterion yields global convexity.

cases.statement: A continuous real function with strictly increasing total derivative is strictly convex; strict derivative inequalities already rule out nondifferentiability except possibly at one point.
cases.proof_strategy: Use continuity of the function on the convex real domain.
sketch_steps: Use continuity of the function on the convex real domain.
Strict increase of derivative values gives strict secant-slope separation.
Apply the strict convexity criterion for the derivative.
No extra differentiability premise is silently inferred from a zero derivative value.

cases.statement: If f and its derivative are differentiable everywhere and f″≥0 everywhere, then f is globally convex.
cases.proof_strategy: The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative.
sketch_steps: The second derivative is the derivative of the first derivative.
Its nonnegative sign makes the first derivative nondecreasing.
The original function is differentiable by hypothesis.
Apply the monotone-derivative criterion for convexity.

cases.statement: If f′(a)=0 with an actual derivative witness and the derivative function has a positive derivative u at a, then f has an unconstrained local minimum at a.
cases.proof_strategy: The first derivative witness supplies continuity and the stationary condition.
sketch_steps: The first derivative witness supplies continuity and the stationary condition.
A positive derivative of f′ makes f′ change from negative to positive near a.
Apply the derivative-sign local minimum test.
This is a sufficient condition; zero second derivative gives no conclusion.

cases.statement: If f has derivative g at every point of [a,b], a≤b, and g(a)≤u≤g(b), some c in [a,b] satisfies g(c)=u; continuity of g is not required.
cases.proof_strategy: Restrict the derivative witnesses to the closed interval.
sketch_steps: Restrict the derivative witnesses to the closed interval.
Darboux’s theorem makes the image of the derivative order-connected.
The endpoint derivative values straddle u.
Obtain an interior-or-endpoint value realizing u.

cases.statement: For a<b and continuous f,g on [a,b] with derivatives h,k on (a,b), some c in (a,b) satisfies (g(b)-g(a))*h(c)=(f(b)-f(a))*k(c). No division or nonzero denominator is assumed.
cases.proof_strategy: Form the endpoint-weighted difference of f and g.
sketch_steps: Form the endpoint-weighted difference of f and g.
It has equal endpoint values.
Rolle’s theorem gives a zero derivative at an interior point.
Expand that derivative to obtain the cross-multiplied identity.

cases.statement: Having derivative u at a is equivalent to the punctured limit of (f(a+t)-f(a))/t as t→0 being u.
cases.proof_strategy: Write the derivative criterion using increments from a.
sketch_steps: Write the derivative criterion using increments from a.
Exclude t=0 in the source neighborhood filter.
Identify division by t with inverse scalar multiplication.
The little-o derivative condition and difference-quotient limit are equivalent.

cases.statement: For every natural n, x^n exp(-x) tends to zero as the real variable x tends to positive infinity.
cases.proof_strategy: Fix an arbitrary natural degree n.
sketch_steps: Fix an arbitrary natural degree n.
Exponential growth eventually dominates that polynomial degree.
Rewrite polynomial divided by exp(x) as multiplication by exp(-x).
Conclude a zero real-variable limit, including degree zero.

cases.statement: For every natural n and real a≠0,b, (log x)^n/(a*x+b) tends to zero as x→+∞.
cases.proof_strategy: Fix the logarithmic degree and nonzero leading affine coefficient.
sketch_steps: Fix the logarithmic degree and nonzero leading affine coefficient.
Logarithmic powers grow more slowly than the real variable.
An affine denominator with nonzero slope has the same eventual scale as x.
The quotient therefore tends to zero for either sign of a.

cases.statement: For a<b, if f,g have derivatives h,k on (a,b), k never vanishes there, f,g both tend to zero from the right at a, and h/k tends to u there, then f/g tends to u from the right at a.
cases.proof_strategy: Both numerator and denominator have the zero limiting form.
sketch_steps: Both numerator and denominator have the zero limiting form.
The nonzero denominator derivative allows a Cauchy mean-value comparison on each short interval.
The derivative quotient tends to the specified finite real u.
Pass the comparison to the right-hand limit of the original quotient.

cases.statement: Every real function continuous on the closed bounded interval [a,b] is uniformly continuous there.
cases.proof_strategy: The closed bounded interval is compact, including the empty case.
sketch_steps: The closed bounded interval is compact, including the empty case.
Restrict f to that compact domain.
The compact-domain continuity theorem supplies a common modulus for every point.
Conclude uniform continuity on the interval without asserting it on all of ℝ.

cases.statement: A real function nondecreasing on uIcc(a,b) is interval-integrable between a,b even if it has jump discontinuities.
cases.proof_strategy: Monotonicity on a compact interval bounds the function by endpoint values.
sketch_steps: Monotonicity on a compact interval bounds the function by endpoint values.
Monotone real functions have the required measurability.
The finite interval measure turns this boundedness into integrability.
The same unordered interval handles either endpoint orientation.

cases.statement: For globally convex f and a<b with derivatives u at a and v at b, the secant slope lies between u and v.
cases.proof_strategy: Convexity orders the slopes of nested secants.
sketch_steps: Convexity orders the slopes of nested secants.
Pass to the right limit at a to obtain the lower derivative bound.
Pass to the left limit at b to obtain the upper derivative bound.
The strict endpoint inequality ensures the secant denominator is nonzero.

cases.statement: A differentiable globally convex real function has a nondecreasing derivative.
cases.proof_strategy: Take two ordered points of the real domain.
sketch_steps: Take two ordered points of the real domain.
The derivative at the left is bounded above by their secant slope.
That slope is bounded above by the derivative at the right.
Transitivity gives monotonicity of the derivative.

cases.statement: If f(x)→u and g(x)→v as real x approaches a with x≠a, their sum tends to u+v and their product tends to uv; no condition is imposed on f(a),g(a).
cases.proof_strategy: Use the common punctured neighborhood filter at a.
sketch_steps: Use the common punctured neighborhood filter at a.
Addition is continuous at the limiting pair (u,v).
Multiplication is continuous at the same pair.
Compose those operations with the pair of convergent functions.

cases.statement: If f(x)→u and g(x)→v≠0 as real x approaches a punctured, then f(x)/g(x)→u/v.
cases.proof_strategy: The limiting denominator is nonzero.
sketch_steps: The limiting denominator is nonzero.
Continuity of inversion yields the reciprocal limit.
Multiply that limit by the numerator limit.
No value of the quotient at a is required for the punctured limit.

cases.statement: If f(x)→b as real x approaches a punctured and g is continuous at b, then g(f(x))→g(b), even if f takes the value b near a.
cases.proof_strategy: The inner limit enters the full neighborhood filter at b.
sketch_steps: The inner limit enters the full neighborhood filter at b.
Continuity of g supplies a limit from that full filter.
Compose the two filter maps.
This avoids the extra avoidance premise needed for a merely punctured outer limit.

cases.statement: A finite punctured limit f(x)→u at a exists with value u exactly when replacing f(a) by u makes the function continuous at a.
cases.proof_strategy: Updating the value changes only the singleton {a}.
sketch_steps: Updating the value changes only the singleton {a}.
The old and new functions agree on the punctured neighborhood.
Continuity at a is equivalent to the punctured limit being the new value there.
Use the update identity to obtain both implications.

cases.statement: If real functions f≤g≤h pointwise and f,h both tend to u as x approaches a punctured, then g tends to u there.
cases.proof_strategy: Every punctured neighborhood inherits the two pointwise inequalities.
sketch_steps: Every punctured neighborhood inherits the two pointwise inequalities.
Both bounding functions eventually enter any ordered neighborhood of u.
The middle value lies in the same neighborhood.
The order-topology squeeze theorem gives the middle limit.

cases.statement: A real function has punctured two-sided limit u at a if and only if its left-hand and right-hand limits at a both equal u.
cases.proof_strategy: The punctured line is the union of the strict left and right half-lines.
sketch_steps: The punctured line is the union of the strict left and right half-lines.
The neighborhood-within filter of a union is the supremum of the two filters.
Convergence from that supremum is equivalent to convergence from each side.
Both sides must have the same target value u.

cases.statement: For every real a and distinct u,v, the function equal to u away from a and v at a has punctured limit u at a but is not continuous at a.
cases.proof_strategy: The exceptional point is absent from the punctured source filter.
sketch_steps: The exceptional point is absent from the punctured source filter.
The modified function therefore has the same limit as the constant u.
Continuity would force its limit to equal its value v at a.
Uniqueness of finite real limits would give u=v, contradicting the premise.

cases.statement: For every a<b, the continuous function x↦x-(a+b)/2 has integral zero on [a,b] but a nonzero value at a. Thus zero integral need not imply pointwise vanishing without nonnegativity.
cases.proof_strategy: An affine function is continuous.
sketch_steps: An affine function is continuous.
Integrate x and subtract the constant midpoint times interval length.
The two contributions cancel algebraically.
At a its value is (a-b)/2, nonzero because a<b.

cases.statement: For every real a, x↦|x-a| is continuous everywhere but not differentiable at a, so continuity does not imply differentiability.
cases.proof_strategy: Translation and absolute value preserve continuity.
sketch_steps: Translation and absolute value preserve continuity.
Suppose the translated absolute-value function were differentiable at a.
Compose with x↦x+a to obtain differentiability of |x| at zero.
The unequal one-sided slopes of |x| contradict differentiability there.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, every vector x equals ∑ᵢ coord_b(x)ᵢ bᵢ for any Fin n basis b.
cases.proof_strategy: Use the basis coordinate equivalence between V and finite coefficient functions.
sketch_steps: Use the basis coordinate equivalence between V and finite coefficient functions.
Apply its inverse to the coordinates of x.
The inverse is the finite linear combination of basis vectors.
The inverse-composition identity gives x.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the coordinates of ∑ᵢaᵢbᵢ are exactly the arbitrary coefficient family a.
cases.proof_strategy: A basis coordinate map is linear.
sketch_steps: A basis coordinate map is linear.
Each basis vector has its corresponding unit coordinate.
Apply the coordinate map to the finite combination.
All coordinates reduce to the specified coefficients a.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, any prescribed family y indexed by a basis b extends to a unique linear map f with f(bᵢ)=yᵢ.
cases.proof_strategy: Send a vector to the same linear combination of the chosen images as its basis coordinates.
sketch_steps: Send a vector to the same linear combination of the chosen images as its basis coordinates.
Uniqueness of coordinates makes this assignment well defined and linear.
On each basis vector the assignment returns the prescribed image.
Any linear map with these values agrees on every basis expansion.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the map constructed from basis images y acts by f(x)=∑ᵢcoord_b(x)ᵢ yᵢ.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand x in the basis b.
sketch_steps: Expand x in the basis b.
Apply the constructed linear map to that finite sum.
Its value on bᵢ is yᵢ.
Linearity yields the displayed weighted sum.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the range of the map with prescribed basis images y is span(y).
cases.proof_strategy: Every output is a linear combination of the prescribed basis images.
sketch_steps: Every output is a linear combination of the prescribed basis images.
This gives inclusion of the range in span(y).
Each yᵢ is the image of bᵢ, so it belongs to the range.
The range is a subspace, giving the reverse span inclusion.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if the prescribed images y are linearly independent, their basis-constructed map is injective.
cases.proof_strategy: Write a zero image as a relation among the vectors yᵢ.
sketch_steps: Write a zero image as a relation among the vectors yᵢ.
Their independence forces each basis coefficient to vanish.
A vector with all zero basis coordinates is zero.
Therefore the constructed map has trivial kernel and is injective.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if the prescribed images y span W, their basis-constructed map is surjective.
cases.proof_strategy: The image of the constructed map is the span of its prescribed images.
sketch_steps: The image of the constructed map is the span of its prescribed images.
The hypothesis identifies that span with W.
Consequently the range is the whole target.
The range characterization of surjectivity completes the proof.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, two linear maps agreeing on all basis vectors are equal.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand an arbitrary vector in the basis.
sketch_steps: Expand an arbitrary vector in the basis.
Apply linearity to both maps on its expansion.
The hypothesis identifies each corresponding basis image.
The resulting values agree on every vector.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, matrix representation sends input coordinates to output coordinates.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand the input vector in its source basis.
sketch_steps: Expand the input vector in its source basis.
The jth matrix column consists of the target coordinates of f(bⱼ).
Linearity combines those columns with the input coefficients.
This is precisely matrix-vector multiplication.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, for chosen source and target bases, every m×n matrix represents exactly one linear map V→W.
cases.proof_strategy: Use A to map source coordinate columns to target coordinate columns.
sketch_steps: Use A to map source coordinate columns to target coordinate columns.
Translate the result back through the target basis to define a linear map.
Converting this map to a matrix returns A.
Injectivity of the coordinate equivalences proves uniqueness.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the matrix of g∘f in three chosen bases is matrix(g)·matrix(f), with the intermediate basis shared.
cases.proof_strategy: Apply f to a source basis vector and expand in the intermediate basis.
sketch_steps: Apply f to a source basis vector and expand in the intermediate basis.
Apply g to each term and take coordinates in the final basis.
The resulting coefficient sums are the matrix product entries.
The factor order is g’s matrix followed by f’s matrix.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, matrix representation preserves addition and scalar multiplication of linear maps.
cases.proof_strategy: Matrix columns are target coordinates of images of source basis vectors.
sketch_steps: Matrix columns are target coordinates of images of source basis vectors.
Evaluation of a sum of maps adds these images.
Evaluation of a scalar multiple scales these images.
Linearity of target coordinates gives both matrix identities.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, for two bases b,c of V, the matrix of b in c-coordinates converts b-coordinates of x into c-coordinates.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand x using b and its coefficient vector.
sketch_steps: Expand x using b and its coefficient vector.
Write each b-vector in coordinates of c.
Collect the coefficient of every c-vector.
The coordinate change matrix has these b-coordinate columns in c.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, for bases b,c,d of V, C(b←c)C(c←d)=C(b←d).
cases.proof_strategy: Expand each d-vector first in c.
sketch_steps: Expand each d-vector first in c.
Then expand each c-vector in b.
Combining coefficients produces the product of the two transition matrices.
Uniqueness of b-coordinates identifies it with the direct transition.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the transition matrices in opposite directions between two bases are two-sided inverses.
cases.proof_strategy: Composing coordinate changes in opposite directions leaves all coordinates unchanged.
sketch_steps: Composing coordinate changes in opposite directions leaves all coordinates unchanged.
The transition cocycle expresses each composition as a self-transition.
A basis has the identity as its self-transition matrix.
Apply this in both orders.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, changing both bases transforms a map matrix by C(c←c2)·M(b2,c2,f)·C(b2←b)=M(b,c,f).
cases.proof_strategy: Change the input coordinates from b to b2 on the right.
sketch_steps: Change the input coordinates from b to b2 on the right.
Apply the matrix expressed in bases b2 and c2.
Change output coordinates from c2 to c on the left.
The composite performs f directly in bases b and c.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, a map f has f(bᵢ)=aᵢbᵢ on the basis b exactly when its matrix in b is diagonal with entries a.
cases.proof_strategy: A matrix column is the coordinate vector of the corresponding basis image.
sketch_steps: A matrix column is the coordinate vector of the corresponding basis image.
The eigenvector equation puts a single diagonal coefficient in that column.
Conversely a diagonal column reconstructs exactly aᵢbᵢ.
Applying this to all columns proves the equivalence.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, every linear functional φ is ∑ᵢ φ(bᵢ) coord_b,i.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand an arbitrary x in b.
sketch_steps: Expand an arbitrary x in b.
Apply the functional φ and distribute it over the finite sum.
The coefficient of coord_b,i(x) is φ(bᵢ).
Extensionality turns this identity of values into an identity of functionals.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the coordinate functionals of any basis are linearly independent.
cases.proof_strategy: Assume a linear combination of coordinate functionals vanishes.
sketch_steps: Assume a linear combination of coordinate functionals vanishes.
Evaluate it on each individual basis vector.
The Kronecker coordinate values isolate the corresponding coefficient.
Every coefficient is zero, proving independence.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, every subspace S has a complementary subspace T.
cases.proof_strategy: Choose a basis of S.
sketch_steps: Choose a basis of S.
Extend it to a basis of V.
Let T be the span of the additional basis vectors.
The full basis gives S+T=V, and independence gives S∩T=0.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, every injective linear map f:V→W has a linear left inverse.
cases.proof_strategy: The images of a basis of V form an independent family in W.
sketch_steps: The images of a basis of V form an independent family in W.
Extend that family to a basis of W.
Send the image basis vectors back to their preimages and the added vectors to zero.
The resulting linear map composes with f to the identity.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, every surjective linear map f:V→W has a linear right inverse.
cases.proof_strategy: Choose a basis of W.
sketch_steps: Choose a basis of W.
Use surjectivity to choose a preimage of each basis vector.
Extend those choices linearly to a map g:W→V.
On the basis of W, f∘g is the identity, hence it is the identity everywhere.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if x is a nonzero eigenvector of f with eigenvalue z, then P(f)x=P(z)x for every polynomial P.
cases.proof_strategy: Repeated application of f multiplies x by corresponding powers of z.
sketch_steps: Repeated application of f multiplies x by corresponding powers of z.
Constant polynomials act by scalar multiplication.
Linearity combines the polynomial’s monomial actions.
The scalar sum is precisely P evaluated at z.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, z is an eigenvalue of f iff z is a root of its characteristic polynomial.
cases.proof_strategy: An eigenvector turns polynomial evaluation at f into scalar evaluation at z.
sketch_steps: An eigenvector turns polynomial evaluation at f into scalar evaluation at z.
For the forward direction, apply the annihilating polynomial to that nonzero vector.
For the converse, a root forces a nonzero kernel vector for f-zI, using the polynomial’s defining property.
This gives a nonzero eigenvector and the claimed equivalence.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, z is an eigenvalue of f iff z is a root of its minimal polynomial.
cases.proof_strategy: An eigenvector turns polynomial evaluation at f into scalar evaluation at z.
sketch_steps: An eigenvector turns polynomial evaluation at f into scalar evaluation at z.
For the forward direction, apply the annihilating polynomial to that nonzero vector.
For the converse, a root forces a nonzero kernel vector for f-zI, using the polynomial’s defining property.
This gives a nonzero eigenvector and the claimed equivalence.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the minimal polynomial of f divides its characteristic polynomial.
cases.proof_strategy: Cayley–Hamilton says the characteristic polynomial annihilates f.
sketch_steps: Cayley–Hamilton says the characteristic polynomial annihilates f.
The minimal polynomial generates the ideal of annihilating scalar polynomials.
Every annihilating polynomial is therefore its multiple.
Apply that property to the characteristic polynomial.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, P(f)=0 iff the minimal polynomial of f divides P.
cases.proof_strategy: Divide P by the monic minimal polynomial.
sketch_steps: Divide P by the monic minimal polynomial.
Its evaluation at f equals the evaluation of the lower-degree remainder.
Minimality forces an annihilating remainder to vanish.
Conversely any multiple annihilates f by the evaluation homomorphism.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, if f and g commute, g maps each eigenspace of f into itself.
cases.proof_strategy: Take x with f(x)=zx.
sketch_steps: Take x with f(x)=zx.
Commutativity gives f(gx)=g(fx).
Linearity of g changes g(zx) into z g(x).
Thus gx remains in the z-eigenspace of f, even if gx=0.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, two endomorphisms diagonal on the same basis commute.
cases.proof_strategy: Apply each composite to an arbitrary common basis vector.
sketch_steps: Apply each composite to an arbitrary common basis vector.
The two results multiply that vector by aᵢzᵢ and zᵢaᵢ.
These scalars agree in the field.
Equality on a basis gives equality of the composites.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the eigenvalues of the operator diagonal with entries a in basis b are exactly the values occurring in a.
cases.proof_strategy: Every diagonal basis vector is a nonzero eigenvector for its diagonal entry.
sketch_steps: Every diagonal basis vector is a nonzero eigenvector for its diagonal entry.
Conversely express a nonzero eigenvector in the basis.
Some coordinate is nonzero, and its eigenvector equation forces z to equal that diagonal entry.
This proves both implications, including the empty-basis case.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, the eigenspaces of an operator diagonal in a basis span the whole space.
cases.proof_strategy: Each basis vector belongs to the eigenspace indexed by its diagonal entry.
sketch_steps: Each basis vector belongs to the eigenspace indexed by its diagonal entry.
Therefore the supremum of eigenspaces contains every basis vector.
It contains their span.
The basis spans V, so the supremum is the whole space.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, adding t times row j to distinct row i preserves the determinant of every n×n matrix A.
cases.proof_strategy: Expand the determinant linearly in its updated row.
sketch_steps: Expand the determinant linearly in its updated row.
The original row contributes det(A).
The extra summand has equal rows i and j, so it vanishes.
The determinant is consequently unchanged for every scalar t.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, multiplying one row of A by t multiplies its determinant by t.
cases.proof_strategy: View the determinant as a linear function of row i.
sketch_steps: View the determinant as a linear function of row i.
Pull the scalar t outside that row slot.
Replacing row i by its original value recovers A.
The determinant is t times det(A), including t=0.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, left multiplication by the elementary matrix Eᵢⱼ(t) replaces row i of any rectangular A by row i plus t times row j.
cases.proof_strategy: Compare the product and the row-updated matrix entry by entry.
sketch_steps: Compare the product and the row-updated matrix entry by entry.
At row i, the transvection contributes Aᵢ+tAⱼ.
At every other row the off-diagonal correction is zero.
The entry identities prove the complete rectangular matrix equality.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, adding t times row j to row i is undone by adding -t times that row, provided i≠j.
cases.proof_strategy: The matrix units in distinct row and column positions square to zero.
sketch_steps: The matrix units in distinct row and column positions square to zero.
Multiplication of two such transvections adds their coefficients.
The coefficients t and -t sum to zero in either order.
The transvection with coefficient zero is the identity matrix.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, simultaneously applying Eᵢⱼ(t), i≠j, to a rectangular system's coefficient matrix and right hand side preserves exactly its solutions.
cases.proof_strategy: The elementary matrix has determinant one because i and j are distinct.
sketch_steps: The elementary matrix has determinant one because i and j are distinct.
It is therefore invertible and its multiplication on vectors is injective.
Associativity rewrites the transformed equation as E(Ax)=Ey.
Injectivity cancels E, giving precisely Ax=y in both directions.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, for every pair of distinct indices i,j and nonzero scalar t, the matrix with t in entry (i,j) and zero elsewhere is nonzero but has square zero.
cases.proof_strategy: Inspect entry (i,j): it is t, so the matrix is nonzero.
sketch_steps: Inspect entry (i,j): it is t, so the matrix is nonzero.
A nonzero term in its square would need j=i as an intermediate index.
The distinct-index hypothesis excludes such a term.
This gives a whole parameterized family disproving the inference A²=0 ⇒ A=0.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, for distinct i,j and nonzero t, the transvection Eᵢⱼ(t) has determinant one but is not the identity.
cases.proof_strategy: A row addition to the identity preserves its determinant one.
sketch_steps: A row addition to the identity preserves its determinant one.
The off-diagonal entry (i,j) in this transvection equals t.
That entry is zero in the identity, while t is nonzero.
Hence determinant one is insufficient to recognize the identity matrix.

cases.statement: Over any field K and finite-dimensional K-vector spaces, a nonzero endomorphism f with f∘f=0 cannot have a basis of eigenvectors, over any field.
cases.proof_strategy: Assume f is diagonal on some basis with entries aᵢ.
sketch_steps: Assume f is diagonal on some basis with entries aᵢ.
The square-zero equation implies aᵢ²bᵢ=0.
Basis vectors are nonzero and a field has no nonzero square-zero scalar, so aᵢ=0.
The map then vanishes on every basis vector and hence everywhere, contradicting f≠0.
